blocks.text: Epididymis is the structure where sperm mature and are stored but is not part of the spermatic cord; it is located on the surface of the testis. The spermatic cord is a collection of structures that pass to and fro from the testis through the inguinal canal. It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the posterior border of the testis and is covered by three fascial layers.

items.text: Ductus deferens, in the posterior part (Option A)
**Three arteries:**
Testicular artery, from abdominal aorta (Option B)
Cremasteric artery, from the inferior epigastric artery.
Artery to ductus deferens, from inferior vesical artery
The pampiniform venous plexus (Option D)
**Lymphatics,** especially from testis draining into pre- and para-aortic nodes, and some from the coverings draining into external iliac nodes.
**Nerves:** Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, and sympathetic fibers accompany the arteries.
Remains of processus vaginalis

The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis muscles, not the external oblique aponeurosis. The inguinal canal is a passageway in the lower abdominal wall.

items.text: **In males:** Spermatic cord and ilioinguinal nerve (Options B and D)
**In females:** Round ligament of the uterus and ilioinguinal nerve (Option B)

blocks.text: The boundaries of the inguinal canal are:

items.text: **Anterior wall:** It is formed from superficial to deep by:
Skin
Superficial fascia in the whole extent.
External oblique aponeurosis
Internal oblique muscle fibers, in lateral one-third.
**Posterior wall:** It is formed from deep to superficial by:
Fascia transversalis, in the whole extent (Option A)
Conjoint tendon, in medial two-third
Reflected part of the inguinal ligament, in the medial-most part.
**Roof:** It is formed by the lower arched fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.
**Floor:** It is formed by:
Grooved upper surface of the inguinal ligament in the whole extent
Abdominal surface of the lacunar ligament at the medial end.

blocks.text: The femoral triangle is an important anatomical region in the upper thigh, where key neurovascular structures pass, and it's clinically relevant for procedures like catheterization and palpating the femoral pulse. The lateral boundary of the femoral triangle is formed by the sartorius muscle. The iliacus and psoas major muscles form a part of the floor of the femoral triangle, not its lateral boundary.

items.text: **Lateral Boundary:** Medial margin of the sartorius muscle.
**Medial Boundary:** Medial margin of the adductor longus muscle.
**Apex:** The point where the sartorius overlaps the adductor longus.
**Floor:**
Laterally: Iliacus and psoas major muscles.
Medially: Pectineus and adductor longus muscles.
**Roof:** Formed by the overlying fascia lata.

blocks.text: The structures are arranged from medial to lateral in the following order (VAN):

items.text: Femoral vein (most medial) and Its Tributaries
Femoral artery and Its Branches
Femoral nerve (most lateral)
Femoral Sheath
**Nerves:**
Femoral Nerve
Nerve to Pectineus
Femoral Branch of Genitofemoral Nerve
Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of the Thigh
Deep Inguinal Lymph Nodes

blocks.text: Femoral Ring- Base (upper end) of Femoral Canal

items.text: **Anterior:** Inguinal ligament
**Posterior:** Pectineus and its covering fascia
**Medial:** Concave margin of lacunar ligament
**Lateral:** Femoral vein
Lymph node of Cloquet (Rosenmüller)
Lymphatics
Areolar tissue

blocks.text: The femoral ring, surrounded by the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, pectineal ligament, and femoral vein, creates a narrow space.
This makes femoral hernias highly prone to strangulation, as the herniated tissue can easily get trapped, leading to compromised blood supply and potential ischemia.
